items.title: 66095_Benny Carter oral history interview
items.q: INTERVIEWER: ...what kind of music it was that you and the Fletcher Hendersons or the Don Redmonds or the Duke Ellingtons would have been listening to...

ctx.x: 'Happy' Caldwells, and Tommy Ladnier, Fletcher Henderson from Cuthbert, Cutpit, Georgia, yes. And gee whiz, it's -- you know -- it was also the melting pot of jazz, you know? New York was ... because of so many musicians from other parts of the country.

Well, one thing struck me in reading Stanley Dance's book which recently came out, which was that a number of musicians who were based in New York described it -- it was much later in their careers when they heard what was described as "Dixieland" music, whatever it is that they mean by Dixieland music, and I was just wondering what kind of music it was that you and the Fletcher Hendersons or the Don Redmonds or the Duke Ellingtons would have been listening to and impressed by. You mentioned Frankie Trumbauer…

Yes, Frankie Trombar, and I didn't -- I wasn't impressed by too much else of the orchestra with which he was playing. I remember he was playing with the Benson orchestra of Chicago, and the record that I did like of his that I think I even heard before I heard "Singin' The Blues" -- now chronologically, I may be wrong about this, but I think I heard "I'll Never Miss the Sunshine; I'm So Used to the Rain" ...
